faqs.a: Use the amortization formula with your numbers, or this calculator. For example, $20,000 at 7% over 5 years gives about $396.02 per month.
faqs.q: How do I calculate my monthly loan payment?

faqs.a: Divide the annual rate by 100 and then by 12. A 7% annual rate becomes 0.0058333 per month. Using 7 directly in the formula would give a payment thousands of times too large.
faqs.q: Why do I divide the annual rate by 12?

formula.label: Monthly payment
formula.note: P is the loan amount, r the monthly rate, n the number of payments

formula.label: Total interest
formula.note: Everything you pay minus what you borrowed

howItWorks: A personal loan is repaid in equal monthly installments that cover both interest and principal. The calculator first converts your annual rate to a monthly rate and your years to a number of payments, then applies the standard amortization formula: payment = P × r ÷ (1 − (1 + r)^−n). Because interest is charged on the remaining balance each month, early payments are mostly interest and later payments are mostly principal.

These are estimates for planning purposes, not financial advice. Real loans may include origination fees, insurance, or penalties, and the rate you are offered depends on your credit score and the lender. Always read the loan agreement and confirm the total cost with the lender before borrowing.
intro: Work out the monthly payment on a personal loan, plus the total you will pay and how much of that is interest. Enter the loan amount, the annual interest rate, and the term in years — useful for car loans, home improvement loans, and consolidating debt.

mistakes.text: The formula needs the monthly rate (annual ÷ 12). Using 7 directly instead of 0.0058333 makes the payment impossibly large.
mistakes.title: Forgetting to convert the annual rate to a monthly rate

mistakes.text: Five years means 60 payments, not 5. Forgetting the ×12 step makes the payment look 12 times bigger than it really is.
mistakes.title: Using years instead of number of payments

mistakes.text: A lower rate usually matters more than a shorter term. On $20,000 over 5 years, dropping the rate from 9% to 7% saves about $1,140 in interest.
mistakes.title: Ignoring how much the rate matters
